title: The Limit and the Poetics of Wonder
Heritage communities and the Faro Convention

author.name: Viviana Matrangola
author.affiliation: Bureau of the Regional Council of Apulia
author.bio: Viviana Matrangola works at the Bureau of the Presidency of the Regional Council of Apulia. From 2024 to 2025, she served as Regional Minister for Culture, the Protection and Development of Cultural Enterprises, Migration Policies, Legality, and Social Anti-Mafia Initiatives. During her tenure, she promoted community-based heritage policies, including the strategic project Care of Places, Arts and Identity-Based Knowledge in Apulia. She holds a degree in Architecture (Politecnico di Milano) and focuses on developing practical tools for place-based care and stewardship in accordance with the Faro Convention. She is a member of the anti-mafia network Libera. In 2017, she received the Borsellino Award.

abstract: This article reconsiders the notion of limits not as a mere regulatory constraint but as an ethical, cultural and political principle for the protection and enhancement of cultural heritage. In a context shaped by globalisation, digitisation and the growing commodification of cultural assets, the limit is proposed as a means of reconciling conservation, public access and the intergenerational transmission of heritage. Drawing on the Council of Europe’s Faro Convention, the study foregrounds heritage communities as active agents in the construction of meaning, in democratic participation and in safeguarding practices. Particular attention is paid to the “poetics of wonder”, understood as a cognitive and civic disposition capable of turning heritage from an object of conservation into a shared experience of memory, identity and collective responsibility. The experience of the Apulia Region, and in particular its strategic project Cura dei Luoghi, delle Arti e dei Saperi identitari della Puglia (Care of Places, Arts and Identity-Based Knowledge in Apulia), is examined as a case study of participatory governance grounded in collaboration between institutions and local communities. The article concludes that only a culture of limits, participation and sustainability can safeguard cultural heritage as a common good and a generative resource for future generations.
